pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Energy can't be created or destroyed

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** The conservation idea is KS3 Physics 'Changes in systems': 'energy as a quantity that can be quantified and calculated; the total energy has the same value before and after a change'. HONEST NOTE: the explicit law wording 'energy cannot be created or destroyed' and the term 'dissipation' are NOT in the KS3 physics energy section — they appear at KS4 ('conservation of energy in a closed system, dissipation'; and 'neither created nor destroyed' appears in KS3 Chemistry's key ideas). So this topic, as described (the formal law + dissipation), STRADDLES KS3→KS4 in England: conservation-as-total-unchanged is KS3; the named law and 'dissipation' are KS4. (Verified by fetch of gov.uk KS3/KS4 science.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** At middle school the nearest is MS-PS3-5 (argue that a change in an object's kinetic energy means energy was transferred to or from it) and PS3.B ('when the motion energy of an object changes, there is inevitably some other change in energy at the same time') — conservation/dissipation are treated qualitatively and the word 'dissipation' is NOT used at MS. The explicit law of conservation of energy and dissipation are HS-PS3 content. So, like the UK, the formal statement straddles MS→HS; assessment boundaries exclude energy calculations at MS. (Verified by fetch of nextgenscience.org MS.Energy.)

- **Operational details:** The child learns conservation as energy BOOKKEEPING — the total stays the same before and after a change — and that 'wasted' energy is not destroyed but DISSIPATED (spread out, mostly as thermal energy in the surroundings). It builds directly on the stores-and-pathways model (mt_Jvg_r4yWaY). Kept qualitative-to-semi-quantitative here; the formal law-statement 'energy cannot be created or destroyed', efficiency calculations and Sankey diagrams are the next step up (Tier C / KS4).

The single biggest hurdle is THE PARADOX the older curriculum created: children are told energy is 'used up' (batteries go flat, fuel runs out) AND that energy is conserved — a contradiction. The resolution, taught explicitly (IOP), is that it is FUELS that get used up, not energy: energy is always conserved, but through every change it tends to spread out / dissipate into less useful stores (warming the surroundings), so it becomes harder to use — 'we conserve fuels; energy conserves itself'. The canonical confrontation is the pendulum (or bouncing ball) that doesn't return to its start height: this does NOT break conservation — the missing energy has gone to the thermal store of the surrounding air via friction/drag; account for the surroundings and the total is unchanged. The teaching job is to make the 'lost' energy VISIBLE as warming of the surroundings, replacing 'lost' with 'dissipated'.

Best taught with a closed-system whose TOTAL is held fixed while stores redistribute, always including the surroundings/thermal store in the accounting, and explicitly swapping the words 'used up'/'lost' for 'transferred'/'dissipated'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional / early-formal, ≈11–12, KS3), reaching toward Tier C.
bestPractices: Use a closed system whose TOTAL energy is held fixed while the stores redistribute — so 'conserved' is seen as a number that doesn't change, not just a slogan.
ALWAYS include the surroundings / thermal store in the accounting — the 'lost' energy is dissipated there; making it visible is the key move.

Explicitly swap the words 'used up' and 'lost' for 'transferred' and 'dissipated' — and separate FUEL (which is used up) from ENERGY (which is conserved): 'we conserve fuels; energy conserves itself'.
Use the pendulum / bouncing-ball-that-doesn't-return as the canonical confrontation: it does NOT disprove conservation — account for the warmed surrounding air and the total is unchanged.
Build on the stores-and-pathways model: dissipation is energy spreading into the thermal store of the surroundings via heating pathways (friction, air resistance).
Keep it semi-quantitative (totals that reconcile) but reserve the formal law statement, efficiency and Sankey diagrams for the next tier (KS4).
keyRepresentations: A locked TOTAL-energy bar above redistributing store bars (the total never changes height)
Dissipative processes: pendulum dying away, ball bouncing lower, car braking to rest
The surroundings drawn as a thermal store that grows as the useful store shrinks
A fuel-vs-energy panel (the battery/fuel depletes; the energy it released is traced into other stores)
commonMisconceptions: Believing energy is 'used up' or 'lost' — the central paradox; in fact fuels are used up while energy is conserved and dissipated.
Thinking the pendulum/ball that doesn't return to its start height disproves conservation — it ignores the energy dissipated to the surrounding air.
Treating 'wasted' energy as destroyed rather than spread out into low-grade thermal energy in the surroundings.
Confusing conserving energy (a physical law that always holds) with 'saving energy' (an everyday call to use less fuel).
Forgetting to include the surroundings in the system, so the energy account doesn't balance.
Assuming a perpetual-motion machine is possible — missing that dissipation always removes usable energy from the cycle.

learn.summary: For 11–12 year olds: energy conservation as bookkeeping — the TOTAL energy stays the same before and after a change, while individual stores redistribute. The central hurdle is the paradox that energy seems 'used up' (batteries go flat, pendulums die away) yet is said to be conserved. The resolution, taught explicitly, is that FUELS get used up while ENERGY is conserved but DISSIPATED — spread out, mostly to the thermal store of the surroundings, becoming too dispersed to reuse. The canonical confrontation is the pendulum or bouncing ball that doesn't return to its start height: this does not break conservation once the warmed surroundings are included in the account. Keep it qualitative-to-semi-quantitative; state the principle plainly ('energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores'), as the objective requires, but reserve efficiency and Sankey diagrams for the next tier. NOTE: as described, this topic straddles KS3→KS4 (England) and MS→HS (NGSS): conservation-as-total-unchanged is KS3/MS, but the named law and 'dissipation' are KS4/HS.

activities.title: Energy budget with a locked total and a hidden-surroundings reveal
feedback: If a learner says the ball's energy was destroyed, prompt them to name WHERE it went — the thermal store of the ball itself, the floor and the air (a little is carried away by sound, which also ends up warming the surroundings) — and relabel 'lost' as 'dissipated'.
If the total appears to fall, point out a store that hasn't yet been included (the surroundings) and ask them to add it so the account balances.
When the surroundings reveal makes the total reconcile, reinforce: nothing was lost, it spread out and became too dispersed to reuse.
For the fuel panel, confirm the distinction: the fuel/battery depletes, but the energy it carried is still present in other stores.
activities.rationale: Conservation is an invisible accounting truth and dissipation is hidden warming of the surroundings; making the redistribution visible against a fixed total lets the learner observe the paradox resolve rather than merely be told it. A live total-plus-reveal format can animate redistribution while the total stays constant, which a static picture or verbal statement cannot animate — offered here as a proposal with that narrow affordance, not a claim that other media cannot teach the idea.
sourceClaims: The 'energy is used up' / 'energy is lost' misconception is resolved by distinguishing fuels from energy: it is fuels that get used up, while energy is conserved but dissipates (spreads out, mostly to thermal stores of the surroundings) and becomes harder to use; the pendulum that doesn't return to its start height does not break conservation — the missing energy warmed the surrounding air.
learnerActions: Run a dissipative process you recognise (a bouncing ball that returns lower each time, a swinging pendulum that dies away, or a car braking to a stop) and watch the useful store (gravitational or kinetic) shrink.
With the surroundings hidden, notice that the energy appears to vanish — exactly the 'energy is lost' intuition.
Reveal the surroundings (e.g. a toggle) and watch the 'missing' joules reappear as a growing thermal store of the air, ground or brakes, so the total is accounted for.
Keep an eye on a TOTAL-energy bar held fixed throughout: it never changes height even as the store bars beneath it redistribute.

In a companion panel, drag a battery/fuel going flat and trace the energy transferred from its chemical store (by electrical and light/radiation pathways) until it ends up mostly in the thermal store of the surroundings — saying aloud 'the fuel is used up; the energy is conserved'.

Read the semi-quantitative joule values and watch the stores (including the surroundings) visibly reconcile to the fixed total — treat any actual numeric summing as optional, since contexts such as NGSS MS exclude energy calculations at this level while UK KS3 does permit quantifying energy.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Lost' energy has not been destroyed: it is dissipated — spread out into the thermal store of the surroundings — and once you include those surroundings the total energy is unchanged. Fuels are used up; energy conserves itself.

activities.title: Bend-a-paperclip prediction and feel test
feedback: A learner holding 'energy is used up' has no reason to expect warming; a conservation learner predicts warming because the work done in bending is transferred to the thermal store of the metal.
If they say the energy is destroyed or consumed, insist on naming where it went and introduce dissipation as spreading out, not disappearing.

If they claim a frictionless machine could run forever and power itself, note that even without friction you cannot get more useful energy out than you put in, and real machines always dissipate some energy to the surroundings.
Keep expectations realistic: the warming is very slight and may be only just detectable by hand, so a small change does not mean 'no energy was transferred'.
activities.rationale: A concrete predict–observe–explain task with a real object surfaces whether a learner has the conservation model, and the felt warming provides direct evidence that work became thermal energy. Physical investigation is welcome as a tangible complement to the visual accounting activity.
sourceClaims: The 'energy is used up' / 'energy is lost' misconception is resolved by distinguishing fuels from energy: it is fuels that get used up, while energy is conserved but dissipates (spreads out, mostly to thermal stores of the surroundings) and becomes harder to use; the pendulum that doesn't return to its start height does not break conservation — the missing energy warmed the surrounding air.
learnerActions: Take a metal paperclip and predict, with a reason, whether the bent spot will feel warmer, cooler, or the same if you bend it rapidly back and forth many times.
Bend it about twenty times at the same spot, then feel that spot (expect only a slight, just-detectable warming, not a dramatic rise).
Explain where the energy of your bending went, using the word 'dissipated' and naming the thermal store of the metal.

Consider the follow-ups: feel a ball and floor after many bounces for a tiny warming; explain why you can't collect that spread-out energy to make the ball bounce back up by itself; and reason why a machine cannot keep doing useful work forever — real machines always dissipate some energy to the surroundings and you can never get more energy out than you put in.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeatedly bending the metal does work on it that is transferred to its thermal store, warming the bent spot — the energy is not destroyed. This is a hands-on instance of dissipation, which connects to why a useful perpetual machine is impossible: real machines always spread some energy into the surroundings, where it cannot be fully recovered to do useful work, and no machine can give out more energy than is put in.

activities.title: Consolidation checks on conservation and dissipation
feedback: If a learner picks 'destroyed', redirect to where the joules went and reaffirm the total is unchanged.
If the redistributed joules don't match the original total, prompt them to include the surroundings until the account balances.
For 'wasteful', confirm: the energy is transferred to stores we can't use (mostly thermal), not removed from existence.
activities.rationale: Checkable judgments consolidate the distinction between 'destroyed' and 'dissipated' and drill the central misconception. A checking format consolidates and checks classification here; it does not by itself elicit the learner's independent construction of the explanation, so it follows the reveal and the predict–observe–explain task.
sourceClaims: The 'energy is used up' / 'energy is lost' misconception is resolved by distinguishing fuels from energy: it is fuels that get used up, while energy is conserved but dissipates (spreads out, mostly to thermal stores of the surroundings) and becomes harder to use; the pendulum that doesn't return to its start height does not break conservation — the missing energy warmed the surrounding air.
learnerActions: Answer: the pendulum stops lower than it started — what happened to the energy? (Reject the 'it was destroyed' option and identify dissipation to the surroundings.)
Complete: energy is not lost but ___ (dissipated).

Redistribute the 'missing' joules to the thermal store of the surroundings so the total visibly matches the starting total — semi-quantitative, with the numeric step optional where energy calculations are excluded.
Decide true or false: 'energy is used up' — and justify the answer.
Explain what 'wasteful' means for a light bulb if energy is still conserved.
activities.intendedInsight: Dissipated energy is still part of the total once the surroundings are included in the account — it has moved to a less useful store (mostly the thermal store of the surroundings). 'Wasteful' means more energy transferred to unwanted stores, not energy destroyed; fuels, not energy, are consumed.

activities.title: Annotated before-and-after as a reference
feedback: Reinforce that the settled pendulum has not lost energy from existence — the surroundings are now very slightly warmer.
Connect the 'unchanged total' callout back to the redistributing stores in the budget activity.
activities.rationale: A static annotated reference can name the idea and label the warmed surroundings, serving as a companion to the live budget bench. Its limit is that it asserts conservation rather than letting the learner watch the total hold during redistribution, so it works best alongside an activity that shows the change.
learnerActions: Study a before/after picture of a pendulum at its start swing versus settled at rest.

Reveal, on the settled state, that the missing energy very slightly warmed the surroundings (mainly the air, through air resistance, and the pivot, through friction); read the 'total energy: unchanged' callout.
Answer 'is energy lost?' and uncover the response 'no — dissipated to the surroundings'.
activities.intendedInsight: Names the idea and pre-empts 'lost' with 'dissipated', pairing a fixed-total statement with the warmed surroundings.

constraints: Keep the treatment qualitative-to-semi-quantitative (totals that reconcile). State the principle plainly ('energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores'), because the learning objective requires it, but reserve efficiency calculations and Sankey diagrams for the next tier (KS4/HS).
Always include the surroundings / thermal store in the accounting — making the dissipated energy visible is the key move; an account that omits the surroundings will appear not to balance.
Explicitly swap 'used up' and 'lost' for 'transferred' and 'dissipated', and separate FUEL (used up) from ENERGY (conserved).

This topic straddles curriculum levels: conservation-as-total-unchanged is KS3 (England) / MS (NGSS), but the named law of conservation and the term 'dissipation' are KS4 / HS. NGSS MS assessment boundaries exclude energy calculations, so any joule values stay semi-quantitative and numeric computation is optional at MS level, though UK KS3 does permit quantifying energy.

Build on the prior stores-and-pathways model: dissipation is energy spreading into the thermal store of the objects and their surroundings through processes such as friction, air resistance, and internal/plastic deformation such as repeated bending (mechanical working that warms things, followed by heating of the surroundings).

Checking/recognition tasks consolidate and check the idea but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the explanation; pair them with the predict–observe–explain and budget activities.
The static annotated reference asserts conservation and should accompany, not replace, an activity where the learner observes the total holding as stores redistribute.
Warming in the paperclip, ball or air examples is very slight and may be only just detectable, not dramatic; feedback must not promise a large or obvious temperature rise.

The impossibility of a useful perpetual machine rests on dissipation (real machines always spread some energy to the surroundings) and on not getting more energy out than in — not on conservation alone; keep this reasoning intact wherever perpetual motion is discussed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Paperclip warming is due to work done in internal/plastic deformation of the metal, not sliding friction; the intendedInsight and feedback attribute it to work transferred to the thermal store of the metal.

Softened an overreaching claim that the paperclip demonstration 'explains why perpetual motion is impossible' to a connection, and qualified the perpetual-motion follow-up so it rests on dissipation and 'no more out than in' rather than on conservation alone.

Legacy entries asserting that 'no static or verbal medium can show the live redistribution' and that a static image 'can't dislodge the paradox' are comparative-necessity claims not established by the cited sources; softened to scoped affordances (what each format can or cannot animate).

The sources support the fuels-vs-energy resolution and the dissipation misconception but do not establish comparative efficacy of one medium over another; efficacy wording kept as proposed/may/intended.

Tension in the original row: the objective/evidence says 'States the law of conservation of energy' while the pedagogy reserves the formal law wording for KS4; kept as a Tier-B-reaching-toward-C treatment rather than silently resolved.
Numeric joule reconciliation is retained only as semi-quantitative/optional because NGSS MS excludes energy calculations, though UK KS3 does permit quantifying energy.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a metal paperclip and ask them to predict: if you bend it rapidly back and forth many times, will the bent spot feel warmer, cooler, or the same — AND why? The 'energy is used up and disappears' child has no reason to expect warming; the conservation child predicts it warms because the work done is transferred to the thermal store of the metal. Then bend it about twenty times and feel the spot.
probeDeeper: Feel the ball and the floor after many bounces — what tiny change might you detect, and what does it tell you?
If the energy is still there, why can't we collect it and make the ball bounce back up on its own?
Counterexample: a light bulb is called 'wasteful'. If energy is conserved, what does 'wasteful' actually mean here?
Someone invents a machine that runs forever with no energy input. What law tells you it can't work, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: The energy isn't destroyed — each bounce transfers some of it, by heating and sound, to the surroundings (the floor, the air, and the ball warm very slightly). The total energy is unchanged; it has just spread out into the thermal store of the surroundings, too dispersed to gather back and lift the ball. So it's dissipated (spread out and less useful), not lost.

errorPatterns.pattern: Energy gets 'used up' and destroyed — once it's gone it's gone ('the ball used up its energy').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on naming WHERE it went (the thermal store of floor and air); introduce dissipation — spread out, not destroyed.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ball's energy is used up and destroyed, which is why it stops.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the bouncing energy is destroyed or consumed rather than transferred out.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Wasted' energy has been lost from the universe, so the total energy decreases ('you lose energy to friction').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Total energy is constant — 'wasted' just means transferred to a store (thermal surroundings) we can't use; account for it in the total.
errorPatterns.distractor: Some energy is genuinely lost to friction, so the total amount of energy goes down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the total falls; treats waste as a leak out of existence.

errorPatterns.pattern: A perfectly efficient or perpetual machine is possible if we remove friction ('with no friction it runs forever and powers itself').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Even without friction you can't get MORE out than in; real machines always dissipate some to the surroundings, so there's no perpetual motion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims a machine can output as much useful energy as it takes in indefinitely, or more.

responseLevels.gap: Says energy is used up/destroyed or that the total decreases; treats 'wasted' as gone.
responseLevels.full: Explains the total energy is constant and the bounce energy is transferred by heating and sound to the thermal store of the surroundings (dissipated, spread out, less useful, not destroyed), and rules out perpetual motion.
responseLevels.partial: States energy is conserved and changes form, but still calls dissipated energy 'lost', or can't say where the bounce energy ends up, or accepts a perpetual machine.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A ball bounces a bit lower each time until it stops. People say the energy 'gets used up' and is lost. If energy can't be destroyed, where has the ball's energy actually gone — and why can't we get it all back to make it bounce forever?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the 'energy is used up/destroyed' model says the energy is simply gone; the conservation child says it's transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy and merely dissipated. The reason tier separates 'consumed and destroyed' from 'conserved but dissipated'.
